conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Rivera, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood by checking on your emotional well-being.  

We’ll use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). It simply asks how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days—nothing more. Your answers stay between us, and there are no right or wrong responses; we just want to understand how best to support you.  

I’ll ask ten gentle questions, one at a time. If any feel hard to answer, just share what you can. When you’re ready, we’ll begin.  

To start: Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft sigh, eyes down]  
I… honestly, I haven’t felt much like laughing. My sister sent a silly meme in the group chat—normally I’d at least smile—but I just stared at it. Everything feels kind of heavy, like I’m stuck in fog. I did crack a tiny smile when the baby made that milk-drunk face, but the laughter part feels… distant.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I mean, I can smile at the baby now and then, but actually laughing—like really laughing—hasn’t happened. Even when my partner jokes around, I just feel too tired and flat to join in.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow head-shake]

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but this week even the idea of leaving the apartment feels like a chore. I did think I might enjoy the online moms’ group, but when the time came, I stayed in bed and skipped it. It’s like the color’s drained out of everything.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... a lot, actually. Last night the baby wouldn't settle for almost two hours and I kept thinking it must be something I did—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I'm not holding him right. When he finally slept I just sat there crying, convinced I'm failing him. Even little stuff, like running late for his check-up, I hear this voice in my head saying I'm a bad mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands]

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing—what if she spits up and chokes when I’m not looking, what if the cough I heard means she’s getting RSV, what if the formula’s too hot even though I tested it on my wrist? Nothing sets it off; it just crashes over me. I know the doctor says she’s healthy, but the worry keeps circling like a moth I can’t swat away.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes, yeah. It’s like a sudden wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen. There’s no real reason; the baby could be napping peacefully and I’ll still feel like I need to run to the crib to check she’s breathing. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most of the time. Even simple stuff—folding a basket of onesies or washing the bottles—feels like a mountain. I’ll look around the apartment and just want to sit on the floor and cry because I can’t see how I’ll ever catch up. I’m managing the basics: baby’s fed, diapers changed, I take a shower every couple of days, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind starts spinning—did I sterilize the pacifier, is the baby breathing, will I ever feel like myself again? Some nights I’m still awake when my partner gets up for work at five. Even when I do drift off, I jolt awake at every little sound she makes in the bassinet. I’m lucky if I get three broken hours before morning.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time, yeah. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly feel this heavy sadness settle in. Sometimes there’s no trigger at all—just this steady ache in my chest. I’ll hear myself sigh over and over without realizing it. I keep thinking I should be happy because she’s healthy and I’m not alone, but the sadness just sits there anyway.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

It’s happened three, maybe four nights this week. Usually once the baby’s finally down and the apartment’s quiet, it just hits me—this wave of “I can’t do this” and the tears come. Sometimes it’s silent, sometimes I’m sobbing into a dish-towel. My partner will find me like that and I don’t even know how to explain why I’m crying; it just spills out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she needs.

You've shared how the past week has felt heavy and colorless-how even small joys like laughing at a meme or meeting friends now feel out of reach. Night after night you lie awake with racing worries, wake to sudden panic, and move through the day overwhelmed by everyday tasks while blaming yourself for every hiccup. Yet alongside the sadness and exhaustion, you remain determined to care for your baby and want to feel better.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient denies genuine laughter and describes persistent anhedonia, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete loss of anticipation and pleasure, skipping even planned activities—maps to "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent self-blame across multiple situations (baby not settling, being late) and describes a harsh internal voice calling her a "bad mom," matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, intrusive, no-trigger worries occurring "pretty much every day," matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>The mother describes sudden panic attacks with physical symptoms (tight chest, breathlessness) and catastrophic thoughts, occurring "sometimes" without a clear trigger.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and emotional collapse, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly difficulty initiating and maintaining sleep due to racing thoughts and hypervigilance about the baby, with total sleep reduced to only 3 fragmented hours—this aligns with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sadness "a lot of the time" with a continuous heavy ache, sighing repeatedly, and persistent low mood despite positive events—closest to "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent crying episodes (3-4 nights in one week) that occur unexpectedly and intensely, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS=25 places you well above the 14-point cutoff that flags probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorse <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, <sym>insomnia</sym>, and <sym>daily crying</sym> occurring "most of the time," together with impaired functioning, meeting core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> to discuss diagnosis and treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> and the risks/benefits of <med>sertraline</med> or similar <med>antidepressants</med> while breastfeeding
3. Schedule brief daily check-ins with a trusted adult who can help with baby care, meals, or household tasks so you can rest
4. Begin simple sleep-hygiene steps: 20-minute wind-down without screens, dim lights, accept help for nighttime feeds when possible
5. Keep local 24-h crisis and warm-line numbers saved (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773, 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline)
6. Return for EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks or sooner if mood worsens, panic intensifies, or thoughts of self-harm develop
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit Day ?? (wk 4–6)

Symptoms endorsed:
- Pervasive anhedonia (minimal laughter, no anticipatory enjoyment)
- Low/flat mood with daily crying spells, often evening onset
- Excessive self-blame and guilt re parenting competence
- Marked generalized anxiety (somatic tension, intrusive “what-if” worries)
- Recurrent panic-like surges (chest tightness, breathlessness) without clear trigger
- Overwhelm with routine tasks, sense of “treading water”
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to rumination
- No current self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)

Pattern: Symptoms present “most of the time” × ≥2 wks; cause functional impairment (skipping social contact, household tasks, daytime exhaustion).

Screening significance: High endorsement consistent with probable major depressive episode with anxious features (postpartum specifier); differential includes peripartum anxiety disorder.

Risk factors identified: Significant mood symptoms, anxiety/panic, sleep loss, self-doubt; protective factor: no suicidal ideation, supportive partner.

Recommendation: Refer for immediate comprehensive perinatal mental-health assessment; safety plan reviewed; emergency resources provided.
